item.title: F.B.I. Arrests Key Suspect in ShinyHunters Hack of Its Own Agents’ Data
item.description:
The F.B.I. has arrested a man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of carrying out the computer hack that stole sensitive information about thousands of F.B.I. employees, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The theft of reams of personal data last month by a criminal hacking group left the nation’s premier law enforcement agency racing to respond as both the investigators and the victims of one of the worst breaches of government data in recent years.

The arrested man is a Canadian citizen and considered to be a primary co-conspirator in carrying out the intrusion, the people said.

Kash Patel, the F.B.I. director, confirmed on Friday that an arrest had been made as part of the bureau’s effort to dismantle the international hacking group. “We will continue to work closely with our partners to disrupt what’s left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate,” he said.

Officials did not immediately release the man’s name or the specific charges against him.

The breach was announced by a hacking group that called itself ShinyHunters, saying it had pilfered intimate details about F.B.I. personnel from the agency’s jobs portal. ShinyHunters threatened more consequences — which many officials and cybersecurity experts interpreted as a plan to release the data publicly — if the F.B.I. did not rescind an advisory warning the public of the group’s cyberattacks, but later backed off.

In the wake of the breach, the F.B.I. vowed to pursue the group’s members, who are believed by security researchers to comprise a loose collective of young English-speaking hackers in several countries across the globe. The group has been active for years and been responsible for some of the most serious corporate data breaches in recent years, often extorting victims for millions of dollars in exchange for promises to not publish stolen private material.

The F.B.I. hack scooped up home addresses, Social Security numbers, sensitive job assignments, details about employees’ family members and more, according to a New York Times analysis of some of the records that was shared by the hacking group. In an internal memo to its workforce after the hack was disclosed late last month, the F.B.I. said it was operating under the assumption that all employees had been compromised in the hack.

Brett Leatherman, the assistant director for the F.B.I.’s cyber division, said this week that a review had determined that the hack was “the result of a security failure of a platform managed by a third-party organization — after a contractor failed to implement a security patch explicitly issued to secure the platform.” That contractor worked for Accenture, Reuters earlier reported.

The bureau has “removed the contractor and taken all necessary steps to both mitigate any further risk and protect our work force,” Mr. Leatherman said, adding that multiple arrests had already been made.

The arrest this week is the latest in a recent string of international law enforcement actions aimed at ShinyHunters. In September, seemingly before the F.B.I. hack, the authorities in the Netherlands arrested a 24-year-old suspected of being affiliated with ShinyHunters, though the group denied knowing him.

ShinyHunters is considered one of the most notorious and capable cybercriminal enterprises in the world. The group is believed to have breached more than 140 organizations and extorted $70 million since last year, Mr. Leatherman said, and has often targeted third-party vendors and cloud-based platforms.

item.title: Top Democratic Group Pumps Millions Into Kansas Senate Race
item.description:
The top super PAC for Senate Democrats is reserving $5 million in advertisements in Kansas’ newly competitive Senate race, signaling that the party sees a serious chance of winning a red state that once seemed out of reach.

The group, Senate Majority PAC, will spend the money on television spots and digital ads through Election Day, an investment to help narrow the gap between Republican and Democratic spending in the state. The top super PAC for Senate Republicans recently diverted millions of dollars to Kansas to defend its incumbent, Senator Roger Marshall, instead of spending in other states long seen as the main battlegrounds, like North Carolina. It is the group’s first foray into Kansas this cycle.

The move, which has not previously been reported, comes as polls show an increasingly close race between Mr. Marshall and Adam Hamilton, his Democratic challenger. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report moved its rating for the Kansas Senate race from “Lean Republican” to a tossup on Tuesday, and a New York Times/Siena University poll over the weekend showed Mr. Marshall and Mr. Hamilton in a dead heat.

Democrats are now stepping up their efforts in Kansas as they try to win back a majority in the upper chamber.

“The gap is closing in Kansas,” Lauren French, a spokeswoman for the Democratic super PAC, said in a statement.

Mr. Marshall, a first-term senator who spent most of his career as an obstetrician-gynecologist, has struggled as President Trump’s approval record has sagged and as fuel prices have remained elevated in the state.

Mr. Hamilton, a moderate Democrat and pastor, has sought to pin Kansans’ financial woes on Mr. Marshall. He has also promised to shore up the state’s social safety net. Mr. Marshall, meanwhile, has branded Mr. Hamilton as an “extremist.”

Republicans have scheduled $13 million worth of television, radio and digital ads in Kansas through Nov. 3, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact. With the additional $5 million, Democrats will have more than $9 million on the books.

The cash infusion will help fund a video advertisement that hits Mr. Marshall for voting to table a Democratic-led amendment that would have directed the Justice Department to release all of the files about Jeffrey Epstein, the disgraced financier and sex offender. At the time, Mr. Marshall called the amendment a “political stunt.”

The ad comes after Mr. Marshall attacked Mr. Hamilton over allegations of sexual abuse by a volunteer at the church he founded. Mr. Hamilton’s campaign has denounced the attack, which came in a television ad, as a “desperate lie.”

The Democrats’ decision to invest more in Kansas comes a week after the top super PAC for Senate Republicans pulled tens of millions of dollars’ worth of ads out of North Carolina, signaling that the party no longer saw a path to keep a Republican in the seat.

item.title: James Talarico’s Absence From the Trail Rattles the Texas Senate Race
item.description:
The last time James Talarico held an in-person campaign event was on Sept. 29, at a fund-raiser in New York City, his second there in two days. A day later he appeared virtually before a Hispanic business group, conducting his talk from a hotel room. He had come down with a cold, he told the audience, which he had intended to speak to in person.

Since then, Mr. Talarico has not done any campaign events — a striking absence from the campaign trail at a time when polls show him in position to be the first Democrat in a generation to win statewide in Texas.

His opponent in the Senate race, Ken Paxton, has been hammering Mr. Talarico over his absence for days, suggesting that Mr. Talarico was hiding some underlying problem that he did not want to divulge. On Wednesday, at a rally with President Trump, Mr. Paxton led the crowd of thousands in a chant: “Where is James Talarico?”

Mr. Talarico’s campaign said that the candidate has been recovering from the flu, and that he would return to the campaign trail this weekend. A spokesman for the campaign, JT Ennis, said that Mr. Talarico had held “more than 100 public events” and shaken “tens of thousands of hands” before getting sick.

The Talarico campaign has maintained a steady presence on social media and in emails to supporters, masking the candidate’s absence from live events. Still, the lack of participation by Mr. Talarico himself in any public events — or even in any private fund-raisers via video — caused even some of his supporters to worry.

Mr. Paxton and his Republican supporters have reveled in the moment, creating “missing posters” and demanding that Mr. Talarico pose for a photo holding a newspaper with the date visible to prove he is OK.

“Still no proof of life,” Mr. Paxton’s campaign wrote in an email blast on Friday. “Texans are still asking one simple question: Where’s Jimmy?”

During his last public appearance, before the U.S. Hispanic Business Council, Mr. Talarico explained that he was concerned about spreading his illness.

“I was starting to feel under the weather a few days ago,” he told the audience. “Last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas and I was diagnosed with the flu and so I’m running a fever and I’m at my most contagious right now. I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail. And so I want to keep everybody safe and you know, if I was passing on this illness to somebody and got someone’s grandmother or someone’s baby sick, I couldn’t live with myself. So I thought the best thing to do was to put safety first and put everyone’s health first.”

Mr. Talarico has not spoken in public since. Early voting in Texas begins on Oct. 19.

item.title: Katie Zacharia Picked as the New White House Press Secretary
item.description:
Katie Zacharia, a conservative commentator who briefly worked at the Department of Homeland Security, has been chosen as the next White House press secretary, according to two people familiar with the matter.

Ms. Zacharia will succeed Karoline Leavitt, who left the position in August. According to her LinkedIn profile, she is currently a communications adviser to Trump Media and Technology Group, which runs Truth Social. She had a brief stint working as a spokeswoman for then-Secretary Kristi Noem at the Department of Homeland Security and is a frequent guest on conservative media.

Ms. Zacharia lives in California and has worked with Fix California, a nonprofit founded by Ric Grenell, a Trump ally, to advance a conservative agenda in the state.

The White House and Ms. Zacharia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

item.title: Donor Says Kimberly Guilfoyle Sought Money From Him to Cover Debt
item.description:
Kimberly Guilfoyle, the former fiancée of Donald Trump Jr., secretly begged a Republican donor to pay her credit card debt while she was waiting to be confirmed as ambassador to Greece, according to an interview with the donor.

The donor, Eric Deters, said that Ms. Guilfoyle had asked him to wire $100,000 to pay off her American Express card just before her Senate confirmation hearing in early July 2025, promising to serve as his “ride or die in Trump world” if he did.

“Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” she wrote in what appeared to be a text message. Communications between Mr. Deters and Ms. Guilfoyle were reported earlier by The Wall Street Journal. Mr. Deters provided what appeared to be screenshots of their correspondence to The New York Times.

Mr. Deters sketched out a tawdry tale in which a member of the Trump family’s inner circle promised access to top administration officials as part of a financial arrangement she insisted be kept hidden. The donor wanted to connect with Pam Bondi, then attorney general, and Billy Long, then the Internal Revenue Service commissioner, for business and personal reasons.

“Every secretary you know defense, transportation, treasury commerce IRS commissioner everyone gets right back to me,” she appears to have written the donor in late June 2025, shortly before her Senate confirmation hearing.

The texts suggest that Ms. Guilfoyle warned him to call her on Signal and keep their interactions strictly private. “You’ll literally cost me my ambassadorship,” she wrote, according to one of the screenshots Mr. Deters shared with The Times.

“Eric, I really wish you would stop papering all these things,” another message said. “It’s really dangerous.”

Democrats immediately pounced on the allegations as evidence of a pay-to-play pattern during the second Trump administration. Representative Robert Garcia, a California Democrat and ranking member of the House Oversight Committee, said such influence-peddling “would be a brazen abuse of power.” Representative Madeleine Dean, a Pennsylvania Democrat who sits on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Ms. Guilfoyle should be fired.

A lawyer for Ms. Guilfoyle declined to comment. Secretary of State Marco Rubio refused to answer questions on Thursday about the ambassador’s conduct as he wound up a visit to Athens.

“Just because some source told you something,” he said vehemently, does not mean “it’s gospel.”

Mr. Deters, who has hosted annual pro-Trump events in Kentucky, is a firebrand with his own controversies. In the interview, he said he retired as a lawyer in 2013 after facing disciplinary actions in Kentucky and Ohio. He is now battling an adversary’s motion to hold him in civil contempt in an Ohio case.

He said that he supported President Trump’s policies, but not his administration’s “open grifting and enrichment,” which he said Ms. Guilfoyle exemplified.

Mr. Deters said he met Ms. Guilfoyle after he began holding an annual “Patriots Day Freedom Fest” in Kentucky in 2020. He said he paid $300,000 to Ms. Guilfoyle, $200,000 to Donald Trump Jr. and $100,000 to Eric Trump to speak at the events between 2021 and 2024.

He also donated $125,000 to a pro-Trump super PAC in 2022, according to Federal Election Commission records.

His relationship with Ms. Guilfoyle seems to have intensified after she and Donald Trump Jr. ended their engagement in 2024 and the president nominated her to be an ambassador.

At that point, Mr. Deters asked Ms. Guilfoyle to help him resolve an issue with the I.R.S. involving his tax deductions. He also wanted her to influence the Justice Department to extradite from Pakistan a doctor who had been criminally charged in connection with botched spinal surgeries and to investigate the doctor’s medical insurance company. He said in the interview that he was representing patients in litigation over their operations.

He promised Ms. Guilfoyle a million dollars if he got a legal settlement, and if Tucker Carlson invited Mr. Deters on his podcast to talk about the case.

In the early summer of 2025, as Ms. Guilfoyle’s confirmation hearing neared, he grew increasingly frustrated with what he saw as a lack of results. He claimed that she never broke through with either Ms. Bondi or Mr. Long.

She insisted that she had pulled out all the stops. “I have never worked harder in my life than to promote and protect you,” the texts indicate that she wrote.

She shared with him a copy of a message she said she had sent to Mr. Long, asking him to look into Mr. Deters’s situation. “Don Jr. and I are very close with Eric Deters,” that message reads.

On June 25, 2025, the texts indicate she wrote Mr. Deters: “Please call IRS commissioner Billy Long wrote me back. BOOM.”

Two days later, the texts indicate that Ms. Guilfoyle said Ms. Bondi was the only cabinet member who did not respond immediately to her — even though she claimed that “we are tight.”

Earlier that month, the texts suggest that Ms. Guilfoyle had asked Mr. Deters for backdated invoices. He sent her a letter on June 11 proposing to pay her $50,000 on July 1 — an amount he wrote that he owed — followed by $50,000 on August 1.

“At the time, I’m her friend, I was considering doing it,” he said in the interview. He described the letter as “bs,” saying she wanted it to disguise their arrangement.

On July 3, six days before her confirmation hearing, Ms. Guilfoyle sent an urgent plea for money, a text indicates. “Banks are closed tomorrow,” she wrote with a praying emoji.

“You could just send it here. It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express that’s all that will show,” she said in the text exchange. She included a PDF with American Express instructions, adding that he would be her “special guest” at her confirmation hearing the following week.

He turned her down, saying his wife would divorce him if he paid.

“Your needing $100,000 urgent unfortunately is not going to work,” he wrote. “I wish you luck.”

Susan C. Beachy and Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: Trump Says He Will Import Russian Diesel Fuel Amid High Prices
item.description:
President Trump said on Friday that he had reached an agreement with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia to immediately import Russian diesel fuel to the U.S. market, despite a Russian ban on exporting fuel.

It was not immediately clear if Mr. Putin had signed off on that deal. But minutes after Mr. Trump’s announcement, the Treasury Department said it was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports “to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market.” The announcement gave Russian energy producers a general license to sell diesel fuel until April.

Russia, a crucial supplier of diesel to the rest of the world, said last week that it was extending its ban on diesel exports until the end of October, amid punishing Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries and other fuel infrastructure. Those attacks, and the export ban, have kept fuel prices high ahead of the midterm elections. Mr. Trump has recently criticized Ukraine for the strikes, saying they were driving up prices.

But Mr. Trump said in a social media post on Friday that Mr. Putin had approved shipping potentially millions of tons of diesel fuel in the coming months.

“It was agreed,” Mr. Trump said, “that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter. Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel.”

The return of Russian diesel to international markets would be a win for Mr. Putin, who has sought for years to break the ice on U.S. sanctions against Moscow’s energy sector.

Despite suffering from the most acute gasoline crisis in decades, Moscow still has an excess supply of diesel. But Edward Fishman, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, said he doubted that Russia could supply as much diesel fuel as Mr. Trump said it had promised.

“The reason Russia imposed an export ban was that Ukrainian strikes had degraded its refining output, necessitating fuel rationing for domestic use,” Mr. Fishman said. “This strikes me as classic Putin — empty promises aimed at sowing further divisions in the trans-Atlantic alliance.”

It is the latest effort by the Trump administration to ease sanctions on Russia in a bid to lower energy prices. At the beginning of the war with Iran, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent lifted sanctions on Russian oil that was at sea, saying that it would add hundreds of millions of barrels of crude to global markets, and would curb prices.

Alan Rappeport and Ivan Nechepurenko contributed reporting.

item.title: Senate Fact Finders Decry Costs of Migrant Detention at Guantánamo
item.description:
In August, a team of Senate staff members inspected the Trump administration’s migrant detention operations at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba. They found 445 government employers assigned to the site, mostly U.S. military members on temporary deployment, and zero migrants.

The findings were released Friday, in the latest report to criticize the cost of the operation. Early in his second administration, President Trump ordered the Homeland Security and Defense Departments to get ready to hold tens of thousands of migrants designated for deportation at Guantánamo. About 850 migrants have been held there since February 2025.

“This comes at a significant cost to taxpayers and undermines military readiness,” according to the report, released by Senator Richard J. Durbin of Illinois, the senior Democrat on the Judiciary Committee.

The study also found the Guantánamo operation has cost more than $100 million, which means the government has spent $118,000 to house each detainee there.

Government officials described the Guantánamo operation as a way station for detainees being deported. The report said the average length of stay for the 850 men was 20 to 30 days. Some were held for months.

Officials with Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Homeland Security Department did not provide comparable costs in the U.S.-based installations that have held the hundreds of thousands of foreign men, women and children since Mr. Trump took office.

Criticisms in the report included a heavy reliance on military personnel for an operation that was ostensibly run by ICE, and questions about whether military or homeland security detention regulations were followed at the prison.

At one ICE facility on the base, a former prison for Al Qaeda and Taliban suspects, detainees did not have a designated place to talk by phone with their lawyers confidentially.

Mr. Durbin released the report ahead of a hearing in federal court in Washington on a challenge by the American Civil Liberties Union to the lawfulness of the offshore operation.

In a statement, he called the migrant operation at Guantánamo “simply unlawful, and worse yet, inhumane” and Trump administration immigration policies “cruel, immoral, and an abuse of taxpayer funding.”

Only Democratic staff members took part in compiling the report. It follows a critical study by the Government Accountability Office of wasteful overall spending practices by the Trump administration’s detention and deportation operations. It included the $2.85 million it spent on tent housing for 5,000 detainees that was dismantled and never occupied. The tents, it turned out, did not meet federal detention standards.

As of Friday, ICE was holding three migrants there, according to two people with knowledge of the operation who spoke on the condition of anonymity. The migrants’ nationalities were not known.

All three were being held in a prison that was built to house about 180 Al Qaeda suspects in 2006. It was refitted for ICE, with bunk beds inside the cells to hold up to 350 migrants.

While the Pentagon position is that the detainees at the prison are in ICE custody, the report said that 23 U.S. military troops are assigned to guard migrants there each shift, accompanied by an ICE officer and two homeland security contractors.

The Senate staff members also discovered that the predominantly U.S. military staff was guided by Army detention policies and that the others reported being bound by ICE rules. But none could show the visitors joint standard operation procedures to resolve any differences their different rules might create, the report said.

The Homeland Security Department already had a separate 100-bed facility for holding migrants at Guantánamo who had been found at sea and sought asylum. But it was empty this week. The Senate staff found that it could hold only 50 men because of longstanding maintenance or structural problems.

The 850 men who were brought from the United States to ICE holding sites at Guantánamo since February 2025 were from 36 nations, according to the study. They included deportees to nearby Cuba, Haiti and Jamaica and others from distant countries that included Eritrea, India and Micronesia.

Representatives for the Homeland Security Department and ICE did not respond to questions about whether the government was planning to expand the detention capacity, consolidate the two facilities or end operations.

item.title: Trump Casts Himself as Columbus’s Protector in Pitch to Italian Americans
item.description:
With fuel prices surging and the war with Iran dragging on, President Trump’s popularity has slipped among nearly every demographic group. So on Friday — three days before Columbus Day and less than four weeks before the midterm elections — he made his pitch to Italian Americans.

“As you know, the radical left communists hate Columbus and they want to abolish Columbus Day,” Mr. Trump told a group of several hundred Italian Americans he had gathered in the East Room of the White House.

“These lunatics that are running,” he continued, “they’re all against Christopher Columbus. But I’ll tell you what, we’re going to be here almost two-and-a-half years. He’s going to be so protected, like nobody’s ever been protected before.”

Columbus has not, in fact, been a notable issue on the campaign trail. But Mr. Trump sought to inject the Genoese explorer into the current political moment.

He stood on a stage beside two large black presentation boards displaying images of white marble statues of Columbus, whose voyages, beginning in 1492, opened the Americas to European colonization. Mr. Trump has had one statue installed on the White House grounds and plans to put another in the Rose Garden.

The first statue, erected several months ago on the north side of the Eisenhower Executive Office Building next to the West Wing, is a replica of the monument that protesters tore down and dumped into Baltimore’s Inner Harbor during the racial justice protests of 2020, after the murder of George Floyd.

Columbus’s enslavement of Indigenous people made him a focus of that reckoning. As The New York Times has reported, more than 30 statues of the explorer were torn down or removed that summer. Cities across the country moved to celebrate Indigenous Peoples’ Day instead of Columbus Day.

A number of Italian American groups viewed such moves as an attack on their heritage, and since then, several have worked to have the monuments to Columbus restored or relocated. In Baltimore, a local artist recruited a team of divers to retrieve the pieces, and his son created the replica that now stands near the White House.

Mr. Trump has cast himself as Columbus’s savior.

“The reason I get all of the Italian vote, I really believe. I didn’t do it for this reason. I resurrected him,” the president declared at the event on Friday.

Columbus, the president added, has “been rehabbed 100 percent.”

Mr. Trump was warmly applauded in the East Room, but it’s unclear how far such a message will travel outside of the gathering of his allies. About 16 million Americans report Italian ancestry, according to the Census Bureau. But polls show voters across the board are far more concerned by the high cost of living than they are by cultural issues.

The president may also have ground to make up with the Italian American community. Over the past year he has attacked Pope Leo XIV, and when Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni of Italy called those attacks unacceptable, he attacked her as well. His administration also picked a fight with Italian pasta makers, threatening crippling tariffs on the industry.

At the White House, the audience cheered and laughed along as Mr. Trump offered his own distinctive impressions of Italian culture.

He opened his speech by praising the late Italian operatic tenor Luciano Pavarotti and introduced another opera singer of Italian descent, Christopher Macchio, whom he described as Mr. Pavarotti’s equal. Mr. Macchio sang the national anthem, and Mr. Trump called him back at the end for “Ave Maria” and the Puccini aria “Nessun dorma.”

Later, Mr. Trump complained that filmmakers had stopped giving movie mobsters Italian names because they thought it was discriminatory: “I said, ‘No, no, you have to understand. The Italians. They love it.’”

The president spent most of his speech regaling the audience with tales of his construction projects all over Washington, and he found an Italian connection there, too. He called up onstage Brett Rugo, whom he credited with building the helipad on the South Lawn of the White House with its granite depiction of the presidential seal.

“He’s a serious Italian,” Mr. Trump said. “He’s a serious Italian and he built the beautiful helipad.”

Mr. Trump called out several notable Italian Americans in the room, including Andrew Giuliani, the son of former Mayor Rudy Giuliani of New York.

But one notable Italian American in the room did not get a shout-out. Sitting quietly at the back was the man at the center of one of the most visible embarrassments of Mr. Trump’s second term: John J. Cafaro, a donor to Mr. Trump, whose firm secured a no-bid contract to install a water purification system in the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

Mr. Trump had promised to make the pool clear and beautiful for America’s 250th anniversary celebrations this year, but the water turned green with algae and became the subject of round-the-clock television coverage and mockery by late-night comics. Mr. Trump blamed vandals, but his administration backed away from prosecutions after failing to produce evidence of wrongdoing.

Among the dark suits on Friday, Mr. Cafaro stood out in an indigo-and-maroon brocade blazer with a metallic paisley sheen.

Asked whether he was still working on the Reflecting Pool, Mr. Cafaro told a Times reporter that he was and that all was going well. “They’re going to start filling it Monday, I hear,” he said. Then he quickly got up and walked away, out of reach of the reporters who were fenced in behind a rope.

item.title: Fort Hood Shooter’s Execution Could Face Challenge in Federal Courts
item.description:
The former Army officer convicted of a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood has exhausted his appeals in the military courts. But he may have options in the civilian justice system to contest his planned public execution by firing squad.

Legal experts say that Nidal Malik Hasan could potentially ask federal courts to step in and stop his execution. That path for the courts to intervene, though, would likely be narrow and rushed, and could involve novel and untested legal claims.

The Supreme Court last year rejected an appeal from Mr. Hasan, who was convicted in 2013 by a military jury of fatally shooting 13 people and wounding 32 more after opening fire at a military processing center in Central Texas. The justices at that time declined to take up his legal team’s argument that a judge’s decision to close part of the proceeding violated his right to a public trial.

But legal experts said the former Army psychiatrist’s lawyers could now file a new appeal to ask the federal courts to block the administration’s plan to kill him on Dec. 3 in a live-streamed execution at the base where he attacked fellow service members. It remains unclear whether he will do so.

Jonathan F. Potter, a lawyer from the U.S. Army Defense Appellate Division who represents Mr. Hasan, did not respond to a request for comment.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the plan on Thursday in an interview with Real America’s Voice, a conservative outlet, saying that the execution would be available to watch “because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”

At the 2013 trial, Mr. Hasan, who was a major at the time of the shooting, represented himself and confessed in his opening statement to being the shooter.

If the federal courts were to weigh in, legal experts said that the case would likely begin in Kansas, since he is incarcerated at the U.S. Disciplinary Barracks in Fort Leavenworth. An appeal could then wind through the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit and arrive quickly at the Supreme Court, likely as an emergency petition.

Legal experts say that Mr. Hasan could challenge the government’s decision to livestream his execution, perhaps by asserting that a public broadcast would violate prohibitions on cruel and unusual punishment in the Uniform Code of Military Justice and the Eighth Amendment of the Constitution.

Courts have rejected requests from private companies that sought to broadcast executions to the public.

In 2001, a federal judge refused to allow an internet company to carry a live feed of the execution of the Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, citing Federal Bureau of Prisons rules that forbid recording or broadcasting executions.

In that case, the broadcaster for adults-only subscription websites argued that the execution of Mr. McVeigh presented a compelling public interest that warranted widespread dissemination of the killing.

But the Supreme Court has not weighed in directly on the question of whether public executions are legal, particularly when requested by the government, experts said.

Public executions have been seen, including by United Nations officials, as a violation of international human rights protections under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, said Eugene R. Fidell, who teaches military justice at Yale Law School.

“This is terrible company for our country to be in,” Mr. Fidell said, citing the authoritarian regimes that have engaged in the practice. But he cautioned that there was “no current legal document that you point to that says this is clearly unlawful as a matter of the U.S. Constitution or any federal statute.”

How the Supreme Court may approach the issue is unpredictable, some observers said.

Less than a decade ago, a majority of the court appeared “deeply attuned” to changes in society’s norms and moral values, including waning support for capital punishment, said Stephen I. Vladeck, a law professor at Georgetown University Law Center, where he specializes in constitutional law, national security and military justice.

Professor Vladeck said he believed that the court would likely have found it “exceedingly difficult to reconcile” changing mores with a live-streamed, public execution, particularly given how long it has been since the last public execution in the United States.

The country’s last state-sanctioned public execution happened nearly a century ago, when about 20,000 people gathered in August 1936 to witness the hanging of Rainey Bethea, a young Black man convicted of raping an elderly white woman.

But the makeup of the court has changed considerably since 2018, when Justice Anthony M. Kennedy, often the key swing vote, retired. Now, the court has a conservative supermajority, with six conservatives and three liberals.

Professor Vladeck described the current court’s approach as “far less sympathetic to those kinds of arguments.” A majority of the justices consider themselves “originalists” who examine legal issues with an eye to how the law was interpreted at the time it was adopted.

With Mr. Hasan, Mr. Vladeck said a majority of the justices may look to whether a particular punishment would have been seen as cruel and unusual in 1791, when the Eighth Amendment, which barred such punishments, was ratified.

“If that’s the test, I think it’ll be quite an uphill battle,” he said, noting that conducting executions publicly was common at that time.

Mr. Hasan could also raise issues related to the planned protocol: death by firing squad. He was shot during his attack on Fort Hood and paralyzed from the waist down. He uses a wheelchair, and it is not clear how the military would execute him.

The Army’s 2023 regulation on executions provides a list of people who can witness one, including “a minimum” of two media representatives. It specifies that no one younger than 18 can be a witness. The regulation, however, can be changed by the Army at any time.

The regulation is far less detailed than the service’s 1944 manual for executions that guided the last firing squad to take the life of an active-duty service member: Pvt. Edward Donald Slovik, who was convicted of twice deserting his unit in combat and was put to death in France on Jan. 31, 1945.

The World War II-era manual, which referred to the firing squad as “execution by musketry,” required an Army band to play a song called “Dead March” as the condemned prisoner was led to a post and strapped to it in “an upright position,” accompanied by a chaplain.

A medical officer was then to place a four-inch, round target over the prisoner’s heart, on a uniform stripped of all rank and insignia, including buttons. An “execution party” of 12 soldiers armed with rifles would form two firing squads. “Not more than four nor less than one” of the rifles would be loaded with blank ammunition, the manual states, and placed randomly on a rack for the dozen soldiers to draw from.

Should an initial volley of six bullets fail to immediately kill the condemned soldier, a second group of six soldiers could be ordered to shoot the prisoner at the medical officer’s direction. A sergeant armed with a handgun could also “administer the ‘coup de grace’” shot by holding the weapon’s muzzle “just above” the prisoner’s ear and “one foot from the skull.”

Following confirmation of the prisoner’s death, the Army band would play “a lively air” as the assembled soldiers and firing party departed the scene.

The manual also instructed: “No photographs nor motion pictures of the actual execution will be permitted except for official purposes.”

Julie Tate contributed research.

item.title: Blogger on Trial: Is a Lewd Image of Shrek Free Speech or Harassment?
item.description:
The American legal system is designed to settle disputes with dispassionate gravitas. Its dignity was tested this week by an image projected on the wall of an Ohio municipal courtroom: Shrek, the ogre of children’s cartoons, naked and posing in a manner more fit for adult entertainment.

The disquieting picture was evidence in the trial of D.J. Byrnes, an independent journalist, in the Cleveland suburb of Willoughby. Mr. Byrnes, who is better known online as The Rooster, faced a misdemeanor telecommunications harassment charge after texting the lewd rendering of the green animated character to a Republican state senator, Jerry Cirino.

Mr. Byrnes is a fixture at the Ohio Statehouse in Columbus, where he often films ambush-style interviews with elected officials. After his arrest, Mr. Byrnes began selling T-shirts with his mug shot to fund his defense, and the case has brought him a notoriety that’s invaluable in the attention economy, where shock and outrage serve as currency.

But the prosecution also raised thorny questions about the boundaries of discourse when digital exchanges and social media platforms have blurred public and private communications.

Mr. Byrnes’s legal team argued he was being targeted for “engaging in political speech about and to an elected official,” while prosecutors said his direct communication was mere harassment.

The trial sprang from a clash between political worlds and generations.

Mr. Byrnes’s Substack blog, also called The Rooster, has 15,000 subscribers and a monthly subscription fee of $12.99. The Rooster often takes a left-leaning stance on politics and sports with Mr. Byrnes, 39, playing the role of journalist-antagonist. In 2024, Mr. Byrnes posed as an Ohio State football staff member and tricked Vivek Ramaswamy into meeting in a parking lot after telling him that he would be speaking with the team.

Mr. Cirino, 74, is a former chief executive of a medical imaging company who pivoted to politics in 2020. Mr. Cirino’s lawyers positioned him as a family man, describing him as a “senior citizen” and repeatedly mentioning his 41 grandchildren. Mr. Cirino said during the trial that he had watched the “Shrek” movie with some of those grandchildren.

Tension between Mr. Byrnes and Mr. Cirino intensified in 2025 when Mr. Cirino threw his hat in the ring for Senate president. Mr. Byrnes started a campaign supporting his opponent.

In May, Mr. Cirino withdrew his bid, and Mr. Byrnes sent the senator gloating text messages.

In one, he called Mr. Cirino “Young Mussolini.” In another, he sent the picture that ultimately got him in hot water: an image of Shrek masturbating that was anatomically, if not politically, correct.

“I don’t know who this is, but I am certain you are a moron,” Mr. Cirino texted back.

Mr. Cirino contacted his local police chief, and Mr. Byrnes was arrested and jailed the following month.

During the jury trial this week in Willoughby, on the banks of the Chagrin River, several content creators livestreamed from the courtroom. The bailiff glared at gigglers as lawyers and witnesses did their best to describe the offending picture.

The prosecution argued that Mr. Cirino had been harassed by Mr. Byrnes.

“There is no legitimate purpose to sending that photo,” said Matthew Lallo, a prosecutor, noting that Mr. Byrnes had not requested a comment for an article or asked to interview Mr. Cirino in his text messages, moves that might have indicated an intention beyond harassment.

Mr. Cirino testified that he has a “tough skin,” but that the messages from Mr. Byrnes were too much. “I said, ‘I’ve had it,’” Mr. Cirino said on the stand.

Lawyers for Mr. Byrnes tried to convince the jury that the crude image was not a taunt, but rather commentary on Mr. Cirino abandoning the leadership race, exhibiting political weakness.

“Cirino had exposed himself,” said William Livingston, Mr. Byrnes’s defense lawyer.

Michael Murray, another of Mr. Byrnes’s lawyers, asked the jury to consider the implications of a politician retaliating against a journalist.

But prosecutors kept their case closely focused. In his closing argument, Mr. Lallo gestured at the projection of Shrek on the wall.

“Tell me how that is not harassment,” he said.

Such skirmishes seem “silly and small,” said Burt Neuborne, a professor emeritus at New York University Law School. But “they are what defines what kind of world we live in. We can either live in a world in which very powerful people get to shut down any speech that annoys them, or we can live in a world in where unruly speech is tolerated, even if it is tasteless, because that’s the price of living in a free society.”

Danielle Citron, a professor at the University of Virginia School of Law and author of “Hate Crimes in Cyberspace,” said that harassment and stalking laws, while rarely enforced, apply to citizens and elected officials alike. She said that such stunts could harm a politician’s mental health and physical safety.

“It can be frightening. It can chill their activities, it can change how they move through the world,” she said, adding that harassment cases are often trivialized when the victims are women or people who do not wield celebrity or political power.

On Friday, after a two-day trial, an eight-person jury found Mr. Byrnes guilty.

Judge Michael Cicconetti told Mr. Byrnes to have no contact with Mr. Cirino and ordered him to pay a $200 fine.

“This was an issue of my personal rights that the statute is supposed to protect,” Mr. Cirino said after the verdict. “That’s all this was about. This was not a First Amendment or free speech issue.”

Mr. Byrnes, through his legal team, declined to comment. His lawyers said in court papers that they planned to appeal.

But Mr. Neuborne said that for The Rooster the loss may be a win.

“If you wanted a blueprint for putting this guy on the map, this is the blueprint,” Mr. Neuborne said.

Alain Delaquérière contributed research.

item.title: For Trump, a Firing Squad on Livestream Becomes the Latest Spectacle
item.description:
President Trump loves a public spectacle. After 14 years on reality television, he has brought one show after another to his presidency — a military parade down Pennsylvania Avenue, the biggest fireworks display ever, even a cage match on the White House’s South Lawn.

Now his administration is planning another unprecedented public exhibition, but one with a macabre twist: livestreaming a firing squad execution.

For the first time, Americans would be invited to watch on their cellphones, laptops and other screens as a convicted murderer is put to death. Never before has an official execution been broadcast live in the United States, turning what in theory is supposed to be the solemn application of justice into an event for an audience of potentially millions.

Under the plan announced this week, those who click online on Dec. 3 would see Nidal Malik Hasan, who gunned down 13 fellow Army soldiers and injured 32 others at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009, shot by rifle-bearing soldiers at the same base on the same day of the week at the same time of day that he opened fire. No limits on who would be allowed to watch were described, even though an Army manual restricts witnesses to an execution.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in an interview with a conservative news outlet.

The idea seemed to shock even some of his colleagues in the administration. Vice President JD Vance cast doubt that it would be livestreamed, telling reporters that “I don’t know that that’s going to happen” and adding that he would not watch if it does. But Mr. Trump said he signed off on it. “Did I approve?” he said. “Absolutely I did.”

The idea of public executions hearkens back to the days when criminals were put to death in front of large crowds in person. And it fits into a broader sense advanced by Mr. Hegseth that the military was better in the days before politically correct “wokeness,” back when women were not allowed in combat, diversity was not a priority, soldiers were not accused of war crimes for aggressive action and his agency was called the Department of War.

No public execution has been conducted in the United States in 90 years, and the decision to conduct this one in front of an audience would put the country in the company of Afghanistan, Iran, North Korea and Somalia. Just 17 executions around the world were confirmed to be conducted publicly last year, according to Amnesty International: six in Afghanistan and 11 in Iran. Even Saudi Arabia, once known for hanging prisoners in public, has not conducted a public execution since 2022.

Even some supporters of capital punishment flinched at the idea of livestreaming Mr. Hasan’s execution, calling it medieval and barbaric. “Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting,” said Senator Thom Tillis, Republican of North Carolina. “Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.”

At least a half dozen other Republican members of Congress made similar statements.

The plan horrified many senior military officers as well. Adm. James G. Stavridis, a retired Navy officer and former NATO supreme commander, agreed that Mr. Hasan deserved the death penalty, but said doing so in public was the kind of thing that “terrible regimes” do, not the United States. “It is not who we are as a military or a nation,” he said.

The Hasan execution order comes at a complicated time for the death penalty in the United States. Tennessee has paused executions after a botched effort to kill Christa Pike, a convicted murderer who survived two doses of a lethal drug. And Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, a Democrat, has indicated that he is seriously considering sparing the lives of all 563 prisoners on death row in California before leaving office in the coming months.

President Joseph R. Biden Jr. similarly reprieved nearly every prisoner on federal death row weeks before stepping down, commuting the sentences of 37 convicted murderers to life in prison. He left just three men convicted of particularly notorious crimes on death row. Mr. Trump, when he took over, ordered the 37 men to be housed in the toughest federal prison conditions, prompting a legal fight.

No one was expressing sympathy this week for Mr. Hasan, 56, an Army psychiatrist who had been assigned to deploy to Afghanistan but decided he was on the wrong side of a war on Islam. On Nov. 5, 2009, he opened fire with a personal handgun at a processing center for deploying troops, shouting “Allahu akbar,” Arabic for “God is great.”

The victims included 10 men and three women ranging in age from 19 to 62. It was the deadliest mass shooting at a U.S. military base in history, and caused a searing debate about the presence of Muslim troops in the armed forces at a time when the United States was at war in Afghanistan and Iraq.

Mr. Hasan, who was shot during the attack and paralyzed from the waist down, was convicted in 2013 of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder. His would be the first military execution since 1961 and its first by firing squad since 1945.

But counterterrorism specialists called it self-defeating to show Mr. Hasan’s execution live, arguing that it could play into the hands of jihadist groups that celebrate the martyrdom of those who kill infidels.

Colin P. Clarke, a terrorism expert who is the executive director of the Soufan Center, an intelligence and consulting firm in New York, said that the administration’s plan was “incredibly myopic.”

“The video of a wheelchair-bound Hasan executed by firing squad will serve as ready-made propaganda for jihadist groups like Al Qaeda and Islamic State,” he said. “I don’t understand how this benefits the United States.”

The SITE Intelligence Group, which tracks jihadist propaganda and messaging, found posts indicating that extremists were already using the pending execution to encourage other radicals. “The crusaders wish to execute the brother publicly,” one message read. “Have they not learned anything from the pages of history?”

The Pentagon has not offered many details about how the execution would be carried out or how it would square with Army rules. The Army manual for military executions proscribes who can witness an execution, including the base commander, a chaplain, two members of the news media, the condemned prisoner’s family and one victim or representative of a victim’s family.

“No person under the age of 18 shall witness the execution,” the manual says.

Public executions were somewhat common in the early days of the United States. George Washington had soldiers he deemed traitors hanged in front of other troops, and revolutionaries hanged two accused loyalists in the Philadelphia Commons in November 1778. Northern states mostly abolished public hanging in the mid-1800s “out of a sense that it was an undignified spectacle,” said Stuart Banner, a historian of the death penalty.

Hangings were moved into prison yards and accessible mainly to public officials, journalists and the well-connected. As the electric chair and gas chamber replaced the gallows in the late 19th century and early 20th century, executions were moved indoors, and were therefore witnessed by fewer people.

“This would be the first public execution in the U.S. in nearly a century, and it would probably be seen by more people than any execution in American history,” said Mr. Banner, the author of “The Death Penalty: An American History” and a law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles. “There are photographs of public hangings from the old days, but no one filmed them.”

The last legally sanctioned public execution in the United States was conducted in Owensboro, Ky., in 1936 when Rainey Bethea, a 22-year-old Black man, was convicted of raping a 70-year-old white woman and hanged in front of a crowd of as many as 20,000 spectators. Another hanging a year later in Missouri was moved into a specially built stockade with only a few hundred select witnesses, though many others climbed trees to watch.

Sonya Lea, the author of “American Bloodlines,” a book about the Bethea case that was published last year, said that it was widely denounced as “a brutal carnival of sadism” and led states to stop allowing large crowds to witness executions.

“There’s a kind of parallel in what we’re looking at now,” she said, “in terms of America’s barbarism and depravity that’s happening — not just a killing by firing squad but cultivating that kind of cruelty as a modern entertainment.”

Eric Schmitt contributed reporting.

item.title: On the Ground — Well, in the Ground — in Kansas
item.description:
At the outset of the midterm cycle, I will admit, I did not expect to find myself in Kansas, a ruby red state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932.

And I really did not expect to find myself as I did this morning: in Kansas, wearing a hard hat, squeezed in a dark and rattly elevator as it dropped 650 feet below ground into a salt mine.

Politics: Full of surprises!

I was in Hutchinson, a city of grain, metal and salt, to write about how Kansas’ Senate election has become so competitive. The race between Senator Roger Marshall, a first-term Republican, and Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor who has thrilled the state’s Democrats, was in a dead heat in the most recent Times/Siena poll.

Outside groups on both sides are plowing money into the race — including $5 million from Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, The Times learned today. The Republican counterpart has promised $14 million to save the seat.

Part of the reason it’s close is Hamilton himself, who is not your typical Democratic recruit. For one thing, he was a registered Republican until earlier this year. He is the founding pastor of the Church of the Resurrection, a United Methodist congregation with 24,000 members. He speaks in the quick, deep, extemporaneous cadence of a pastor with a podcast, which is what he is (or was — the podcast went on hiatus just before he began running for Senate).

And he was really excited about visiting this salt mine. I jumped at the chance to join his tour, unsure exactly where the mine fit into his campaign but eager for a chance to spend a little bit more time with a figure who is suddenly commanding national attention.

Hamilton, his wife, LaVon, his pastor friend and a handful of campaign staff met Jeff Ollenburger, the president of a company called UV&S that has turned the empty chambers, far below the ground, into storage space. The mine sits in a salt vein that, Ollenburger explained, is part of a salt cavity that runs from Kansas City to New Mexico.

Hamilton pulled a chunk of salt out of his pocket — salt that he said came from these mines. He told me he always carries it with him and marveled at its age: 270 million years old.

“I’ve been praying that I could be salt and light for years,” Hamilton said, referencing the Sermon on the Mount that Jesus delivers in the Gospel of Matthew.

When we got out of the elevator, I realized, to my surprise, that we had no cellphone service. We were in a warren of rooms the size of football fields, carved out of salt that had been mined here since the 1920s. There were no attack ads down here, no digital streaming wars. What there were, interestingly, were movies — UV&S has become a mecca for storing the reels of Hollywood’s greatest films.

“Where is the ark of the covenant?” joked Hamilton.

We toured the mines, taking in the vinegary scent of aging film. (Some film was stored in chilled space to help preserve it.) Hamilton seemed to lose himself in curiosity. At one point, he even licked a wall. “You know,” he said, “this tastes just like salt.”

There was, of course, a video to shoot for social media. Hamilton asked one of his aides to film him talking to the camera about the salt he carries, the Sermon on the Mount, and the history of the mines here.

“My prayer is just, ‘Lord, as I feel in my pocket, Lord, help me to be a blessing to other people. Help me to enhance their lives, whoever I’m speaking to, whatever I’m doing, as I’m seeking to run for the Senate,’” Hamilton said, and he urged anyone watching to come visit Hutchinson themselves.

Then he headed back into the elevator, back into the light, and back to the campaign trail.

Debate Week

A busy week of Senate battleground debates culminated in some fiery exchanges last night, with candidates getting personal as they went at each other.

Senator Jon Ossoff, the Democratic incumbent, hammered the Republican challenger Mike Collins over his history of employing aides who have espoused white nationalist and antisemitic views. “You’ve hired half the Third Reich,” Ossoff said. He later added, “If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club.”

Collins, for his part, called Ossoff a “trust fund kid who’s never had a job in his life.”

When the topic of Flock cameras that monitor traffic and read license plates came up, Mike Rogers, the Republican, wondered aloud why Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat, would oppose technology that could catch people suspected of being terrorists. “Well, if you have someone in your family that might be on the, on the watch list …”

“Go ahead and say it,” responded Dr. El-Sayed, an Egyptian American who would be the country’s first Muslim senator. “You’ve been tiptoeing around it the whole time.”

Troy Jackson, the Democratic challenger, accused the Republican incumbent, Senator Susan Collins, of profiting off the war in Iran. “Senator Collins and her husband are making money — more — off this war, and so are a whole bunch of other people,” Jackson claimed. “And that’s why this doesn’t stop.”

“That is absolutely outrageous,” Collins said, pointing a finger at Jackson. “And you owe me an apology.”

Jackson replied, “No, you owe me an apology.”

For more: Read takeaways from all three debates.

Get Caught Up

Democratic lawmakers, and a handful of Republicans, decried the Pentagon’s plan to livestream the execution of the gunman who killed 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009.

Vice President JD Vance said he would not watch the execution and cast doubt on whether the Pentagon’s plan would go forward at all.

The county board in Arlington, Va., sued to block the construction of Trump’s proposed 250-foot triumphal arch.

Trump has begun sending $500 “refund” checks, along with a signed letter taking credit for the payments, to nearly a million Americans who get their health insurance through the Affordable Care Act.

Katie Zacharia, a conservative commentator who briefly worked at the Department of Homeland Security, has been chosen as the next White House press secretary.

James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee in Texas, returned to the campaign trail after a nearly 10-day absence. He said he had been recovering from a bad case of the flu.

The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan group that assesses elections, shifted its ratings on 18 House races today, all in Democrats’ favor.

Trump again referred to El-Sayed as “Mohammed,” explaining he was doing so because “I feel like it.”

In One Graphic

Trump has attacked the integrity of U.S. elections on more than 70 percent of the days since he returned to office. On social media and in speeches, the president repeats a litany of false claims: that he actually won the 2020 election, that Democrats use undocumented immigrants to “cheat” in elections, that mail-in ballots produce fraudulent results.

Karen Yourish and Arfa Momin looked back at every day of Trump’s second term and documented all of the instances where he cast doubt on elections. By their count, it has happened on 440 days.

What We’re Watching

Trump is headed to Syracuse, N.Y., tonight to rally for Bruce Blakeman, the Republican nominee for governor. It is Trump’s third rally this year in his home state, where registered Democrats outnumber Republicans two to one.

The left’s biggest surrogates are hitting the trail: Bernie Sanders will be in Maine this weekend with Troy Jackson, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez will campaign next week in Michigan with El-Sayed.

Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, will travel to Bucks County, Pa., where Democrats are hoping to flip the First District. Mike Johnson, the Republican House speaker, campaigned in the district earlier this week.

In South Carolina’s Senate race, Darline Graham and Annie Andrews will face off in a debate on Sunday night.

Do you think Democrats have a shot in Iowa? Will Republicans hold their seat in Maine? Our new interactive tool lets you decide how the Senate battleground races will turn out.

ONE LAST THING

… to see the dueling narratives on TikTok about Talarico.

The Times analyzed all the posts about the Texas Senate race over one 24-hour span in September, using a collection of keywords and hashtags about the candidates. We found that about 70 percent of videos about the race focused on Talarico — both positive and negative — compared with about 30 percent that focused on his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton.

This laser focus on Talarico, Republican strategists say, is partly by design.

“If I can make this a referendum on my opponent, that’s always a good place to be,” Vinny Minchillo, a Texas-based Republican consultant, said. “It is a back alley knife fight with rusty knives.”

Taylor Robinson contributed to this newsletter.

Read past editions of the newsletter here.

If you’re enjoying what you’re reading, please consider recommending it to others. They can sign up here.

Have feedback? Ideas for coverage? We’d love to hear from you. Email us at onpolitics@nytimes.com.

item.title: Off-Duty ICE Agent Is Shot and Arrested After Sleeping on Lawn in California
item.description:
An off-duty Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent was shot early Friday after he was found sleeping on the lawn of a home in Fresno, Calif., the authorities said.

The Fresno Police Department received calls reporting a gunshot in a neighborhood shortly after 3 a.m. local time, the department said in a statement on Friday.

David Gonzalez, an ICE agent from Texas, had been sleeping on the lawn when a woman returned to her house and saw him, the police said. The woman told her father, who was inside the house.

The father, 72, woke up Mr. Gonzalez, who appeared “intoxicated and agitated,” the police said. Mr. Gonzalez then assaulted the 72-year-old man, causing several “visible injuries,” and then assaulted his daughter when she tried to intervene, the police said.

The woman’s father then pulled out a firearm and shot Mr. Gonzalez once, the police said. The woman’s boyfriend, an off-duty police officer, arrived soon after and handcuffed Mr. Gonzalez, the police said.

Mr. Gonzalez, 32, was charged with felony assault and vandalism, the Fresno Police Department said. He was taken away from the scene in an ambulance and received treatment while an investigation was carried out, the police said.

ICE did not immediately return a request for comment. The Department of Homeland Security referred questions about Mr. Gonzalez to the Fresno Police Department.

The 72-year-old man is not facing charges, the police said, and he legally owned his weapon.

The police did not say why Mr. Gonzalez was in Fresno. Lt. Brian Pierce, a spokesman for the Fresno Police Department, declined to comment on the case.

At least four members of the Fresno City Council responded to the shooting with statements denouncing what they described as an increased ICE presence in the Central Valley, home to many migrant farm workers.

“ICE is operating outside the limits of its legal authority, and the people of Fresno are paying the price,” Nelson Esparza, the City Council president, wrote in a statement on social media.

item.title: This Robot Will Deliver Your Food, if It Doesn’t Get Smashed First
item.description:
The food delivery robot was planted facedown on a downtown Los Angeles sidewalk, its four wheels askew, when Jag Gonzalez came to its rescue.

Small, squat and controlled by A.I., the machine can do most tasks on its own — except stand up.

“It wasn’t my first one I’ve ever flipped over,” said Mr. Gonzalez. “I had been seeing this abuse so much.”

Mr. Gonzalez, 28, sent the robot on its way and headed to a movie, where he told friends about the rescue. But three hours later, there it was again on a new corner: the same droid, taking a beating from the Adidas-clad foot of a tottering pedestrian.

Mr. Gonzalez tried to stop the perpetrator. But the man crouched to look the robot straight in its LED eyes.

“You suck,” he said — and delivered a final kick to its midsection.

In American cities big and small, legions of similar machines are carting around takeout orders of sushi, pizza and White Castle’s chicken rings and testing the question of whether humans and robots can coexist.

Early signs are not promising. Throughout 2026, Americans have kicked, tipped and walloped the food robots — the most tangible incarnation of A.I. to reach their front steps.

Within the past year: A crowd in Los Angeles encircled and pounded a delivery robot; a man in Miami tried to hurl one off a bridge; another attacked one in the street; in Sacramento, three men filmed themselves toppling and slamming a robot on the sidewalk, racking up nearly 2.5 million views on social media.

The caption? “Protecting the world from A.I.”

Some attacks are vigilantism and some may be mere knuckleheadism, the thrill of attacking the defenseless. Eunisses Hernandez, a Los Angeles City Council member whose district is swarmed by robots, said the trend had a clear message.

“Because of how heightened people’s senses are to corporations and to the advancement of A.I. technology, people feel like this is the closest they get to some of that other than online,” she said. “People feel left behind.”

Roughly 5,000 robots deliver nationwide, mostly without incident, said Dan Ives, a partner and tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, an investment bank. Over the next three years, that’s expected to swell to 8,000, and analysts predict the industry will generate more than $5 billion in the U.S., Mr. Ives added.

More than half a million could be operating worldwide by 2035, according to estimates from Transforma Insights, a research firm. And those robots could be delivering more than just food as companies forge ahead with expansion plans.

Right now, the bots aren’t exactly cash cows. Serve Robotics, one of few publicly traded operators, lost more than $100 million last year. It brought in $2.7 million. But Serve and other top companies are backed by such names as Nvidia, leader of the A.I. boom; Sam Altman, who helms OpenAI; Uber and the A.I. giant Nebius — tech heavyweights that have poured in hundreds of millions.

Through partnerships with DoorDash, Uber Eats and other food delivery platforms, companies are operating in at least 10 metro areas. Using A.I., the bots assess traffic and plan routes. They sidle up to restaurants, pop open insulated compartments and collect orders. Some can stash up to six large pizzas. A variety of buzzes — texts, calls, notifications — alerts customers to their arrival.

With bright, white circles for eyes and human names emblazoned on their sides, Serve Robotics’ droids were designed to look innocuous, said Ali Kashani, the company’s chief executive.

“Vandalism and societal acceptance were very top-of-mind,” he added.

But looks go only so far. Some freewheeling robots have become agents of chaos, blocking ambulances, clogging walkways, colliding with trucks and trains and, along the way, igniting frenzied robophobia. In Los Angeles, Miami, Philadelphia and more, the robots have faced vandalism this past year, according to police departments and encounters shared on social media.

Intentionally damaging property is a crime, but arrests are few and statistics recording the reign of terror are scant.

At the hands of a vandal, robots are helpless, unable to call authorities. That makes it difficult for police to track abuse, said Jasmine Reilly, a spokeswoman for the Philadelphia Police Department. “Unless people report it,” she said, “we won’t know anything about it.”

Several companies have human supervisors who watch from afar, aiding robots in their hour of need. A call to the police is “very rare,” said Mr. Kashani of Serve. “We actually don’t want to be using police resources for this.”

Sometimes, their assistance is unavoidable. Hapless robots have wandered into peril on their own, falling down stairs, plowing through glass and going haywire on sidewalks. At least one has collided with a self-driving car. Another breached an active fire zone.

“ROBOT IS STILL ON THE SCENE,” a police dispatcher in Miami wrote in January, responding to a machine that rammed a 15-story building, shattering a window.

But robot mayhem is low on the list for officers. As Tom Saggau, a spokesman for the Police Protective League union in Los Angeles, put it: “This is Los Angeles. If we’ve got to start worrying about that, we’re in deep” — uh — trouble.

The misadventures and misfortunes of delivery robots are well-chronicled on social media — sometimes by abusers themselves. (See:@FilmTheRobotsLA across platforms).

Among the lowlights: a brutal, late-night pile-on in Los Angeles after last year’s World Series (700,000+ views) and one humiliation in Philadelphia, where an oblivious bot rolled around with “destroy me plz” inked across what one might consider its forehead (3,000+ likes).

The hope of online virality can motivate abuse, said Lindsay Ouellette a psychology professor at LaSalle University in Philadelphia who studies human-robot relations. “We know that controversial content gets clicks,” she said.

Those clicks come, in part, because robot abuse strikes a chord, tapping into “fear that people have around their jobs and A.I. taking over,” she added.

Robot couriers help restaurants cut labor costs by replacing delivery workers. But robotics companies note they also create some jobs. Every 10 Coco Robotics droids generate one human engineering role, said Zach Rash, the Los Angeles-based company’s chief executive. The robots also benefit communities in other ways, he added. Coco’s bots scan sidewalks, sharing data with an app that helps the visually impaired avoid obstacles.

Robotics companies said they worked with local officials and pedestrian, biking and disability groups, among others, to ensure the machines rolled into cities smoothly.

But the robots’ ability to collect data is a flashpoint for some residents who, local officials said, feel watched by machines that appeared suddenly, with little regulation.

In Glendale, Calif., a Los Angeles suburb, Mayor Ardashes Kassakhian said the robots’ arrival was “like something out of a sci-fi movie.” In Chicago, they “emerged overnight,” said Daniel La Spata, an alderman in the city’s First Ward.

Mr. Kassakhian has proposed a pause on the rollout; in Mr. La Spata’s ward, residents overwhelmingly voted to block robots from expanding onto more streets. Both officials say a slew of questions must be answered: Should robots be banned from high foot-traffic areas? Are they displacing any human jobs?

In Los Angeles, Ms. Hernandez, the councilwoman, sponsored a motion passed by City Council last year that asks the Los Angeles Department of Transportation to examine the robots’ impact — on pedestrians, accessibility and more — and suggest improvements.

“There’s a lot of people who are disgruntled,” she said. Ms. Hernandez believes they are “recognizing what it is,” she said, “and vandalizing it out of frustration.”

It doesn’t take much, in fact, for some to resort to violence. In a survey of college students, Ms. Ouellette, the psychology professor, asked: What would it take for you to kick a delivery robot?

When offered $100? One in five said they would consider aggression.

Battery and bedlam aside, the robots are, to many, already a fact of life — as normal as streetlights and the robotaxis stopped at them, said Mr. Gonzalez, the Los Angeles man who rescued, momentarily anyway, the delivery bot.

Walking through downtown Los Angeles, where the robots roam, Mr. Gonzalez paused and said: “It’s the future.”

item.title: Could the Oregon Governor’s Race Be a Republican Hope?
item.description:
National Republicans, facing stiff headwinds in some of the most conservative parts of the country, see a ray of hope in an unlikely state: Oregon.

With Oregon’s ballots set to hit the mail next week, Gov. Tina Kotek’s quest for re-election in one of the country’s most consistently liberal states is at risk of being derailed by a conservative, anti-abortion Republican, State Senator Christine Drazan.

Conservatives are not exactly surging statewide in the land of protest frogs and craft beer. But Ms. Kotek, a first-term Democratic governor, has managed to become almost as unpopular among her constituents as President Trump, whom they denounce routinely on the streets.

“If this were just a straight-up question, ‘Do you want Tina Kotek to have another four years or not?’ she would get destroyed,” said John Horvick, senior vice president at DHM Research, a polling firm in Portland, Ore.

Oregonians haven’t elected a Republican governor since 1982, and Ms. Kotek would seem well positioned to continue that streak. She went toe-to-toe with Mr. Trump last fall over his efforts to deploy National Guard troops to Portland amid immigration demonstrations and she has already defeated Ms. Drazan once.

Yet polls show this race between Ms. Kotek and Ms. Drazan essentially tied. A recent statewide poll conducted by Mr. Horvick’s firm for Oregon Public Broadcasting found that 60 percent of potential voters viewed Ms. Kotek unfavorably, versus 63 percent for the president.

The situation in Oregon has echoes in another blue state: Minnesota. There, the Democratic lieutenant governor, Peggy Flanagan, is struggling for a clear lead in her Senate race against a Republican newcomer, Michele Tafoya, and the progressive attorney general, Keith Ellison, is in danger of losing his re-election.

In both states, the pivotal issues are local, not national — a lingering social welfare fraud scandal in Minnesota and a sense in Oregon that the state’s post-pandemic malaise is not lifting, even as the cost of living goes up.

There’s also a political truth that Democrats risk forgetting even in a potential blue-wave year: Performance matters.

Ms. Kotek ran four years ago pledging to reduce homelessness, supercharge housing production and improve public schools, but the progress has been far slower than promised.

Ms. Kotek pushed through changes to ease construction of affordable homes, and housing starts have begun rising after falling early in her term. Still, they are nowhere near her goal of 36,000 houses a year, and the homeless population is substantially higher than when she took office.

In 2024, the most recent data available, Oregon’s fourth graders posted the fourth worst performance in reading in the country. This year, just 42 percent of third graders scored as proficient at reading and writing.

“Tina Kotek told Oregonians that she would solve the problems and challenges facing our state,” Ms. Drazan said at their first debate earlier this month. “She hasn’t.”

Priscilla Southwell, a political science professor emeritus at the University of Oregon, said she thinks Ms. Kotek “has actually done a good job with what she’s been handed.” But, she added, Oregon “is more purple than people may realize, and these are hard economic times.”

Some progressives have joined the criticism chorus, frustrated by the business-friendly recommendations from a bipartisan “prosperity council” she convened to tackle economic issues and her 2025 calls to reduce a tax on high earners that funds one county’s universal preschool program.

In a second term, Ms. Kotek has promised to bring Oregon schools up to the national average for instructional time, expand child care and affordable housing, create a new state commerce department to spur economic growth, and halt new data centers until the state passes its own standards. Her campaign pitch unwittingly echoes Vice President JD Vance’s: Just give her “more time.”

“I’m not satisfied, either,” Ms. Kotek said at the recent debate.

When it comes to Ms. Drazan, Ms. Kotek has been mostly focused on the president. One ad deemed the Republican his “right hand.” At the debate, the governor mentioned him so many times Ms. Drazan accused her of helping at-home viewers play a drinking game.

In the State Legislature, Ms. Drazan sponsored bills to bar transgender girls from playing on girls’ sports teams and to end Oregon’s pioneering universal vote-by-mail system. She opposes abortion, though she has said she would not challenge Oregon’s statutory abortion protections, which are among the strongest in the country.

Last fall, as Mr. Trump’s attempt to deploy federalized National Guard troops to Portland prompted demonstrations and a court challenge, Ms. Drazan accused state and local leaders of allowing “violent mobs and domestic terrorists” threaten federal agents. She’s banking on Oregonians, particularly suburban and rural voters, being tired of the homeless camps and empty storefronts in Portland lingering six years after the pandemic.

The candidates agree that Oregonians are hurting financially. Ms. Kotek has emphasized decisions made in Washington. Ms. Drazan points to the State Capitol.

The two candidates have a rivalry that stretches back before the 2022 campaign, when Ms. Kotek won 47 percent to 44 percent of votes. That lent a personal edge to the frowns, head shakes and mutual accusations of dishonesty that peppered their first debate.

As the State House Republican leader, Ms. Drazan used walkouts and other procedural tactics to block or slow Ms. Kotek’s legislative agenda. In 2021, Ms. Drazan accused Ms. Kotek of reneging on a deal to give Republicans equal representation on a redistricting committee in exchange for ending their delaying tactics.

History suggests Democrats and independents will “come home” to Ms. Kotek. Polls around this time four years ago also suggested a closer race than the final result., and a new poll from The Oregonian shows movement toward the governor and a slight Kotek lead. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report still says the race leans Democratic in a state where Republicans make up just 24 percent of the electorate.

Ms. Kotek also has a substantial financial advantage — her campaign has $3.4 million to spend, compared with nearly $2 million for Ms. Drazan’s. And Ms. Drazan has yet to receive any contributions from the one person in Oregon who could close that gap: Phil Knight, the Nike co-founder and frequent Republican donor.
