item.title: 7 Coffins Are Found Near North Dakota Governor’s Residence
item.description:
Last May, contractors were upgrading the security fences and driveway at the governor’s residence in North Dakota when they made a discovery that brought the work to a standstill. In the southwest corner of the grounds, where a cemetery had once been, they unearthed what appeared to be human remains and coffin fragments.

Over the next four months, what started as a landscaping and construction job in the state capital, Bismarck, turned into an examination of the state’s history. This week, officials in Gov. Kelly Armstrong’s administration announced the results of an analysis of the remains: They were two women, two men, two teenage boys and a toddler.

The seven sets of remains appear to have been overlooked when bodies at the former cemetery were exhumed after 1877 and moved to new cemeteries during Bismarck’s early settlement period, the state Office of Management and Budget said in a statement.

“Many were already reinterred to somewhere else,” Jen Raab, a spokeswoman for the office, said in an interview. “We didn’t know there were still some there.”

The discovery on May 19 set in motion a wide-ranging project that has played out at the nexus of science, history and spirituality in Bismarck, a onetime frontier town that is now a city of about 78,000.

The state Legislature last year approved $2.35 million in security upgrades at the governor’s residence, which sits on the grounds of the Capitol. After the remains were discovered, archaeologists were dispatched to the site to conduct surveys with ground-penetrating radar. They detected more than 80 anomalies in the earth, leading to the recovery of seven sets of remains and an empty wood box, the Office of Management and Budget said.

A chaplain will organize a ceremonial handling of the remains, which will be reburied next year, Ms. Raab said.

In a statement on Friday, Mike Nowatzki, a spokesman for the governor’s office, said Governor Armstrong “wants to ensure the remains are treated with appropriate care and respect.”

The discovery of the remains generated interest in the former cemetery and how its long-buried dead ended up intersecting with modern city life.

Historians scoured archival newspaper clippings for death notices to help tell the story of the burials, which were held on the grassy knoll from 1872 through 1877 — a period that coincides with the renaming of the town, formerly known as Edwinton, to Bismarck in 1873.

The cemetery did not have an official name. Townspeople generally called it “the graveyard on the hill,” according to the state archives.

“It was far out of town,” said Lindsay K. Meidinger, the deputy archivist at the North Dakota State Archives.

One person known to have been buried there was a woman named Sophie deMarsh. The Bismarck Weekly Tribune reported in January 1877 that she “suffered through three days labor, but will probably recover.”

She did not. She died in the next month, the newspaper reported, according to archival clippings provided by Ms. Meidinger.

By the end of 1877, the old newspaper clippings reported that a section of the burial ground was going to be sold to make way for a railroad. The cemetery, and those at rest there, had to find a new home. So bodies were moved to other cemeteries.

But not all of them, as the newspaper reported over the decades that followed. As the city developed, more of the buried dead were found, their resting places inadvertently intertwined with newly laid streets and railroad tracks.

In 1903, at least 13 bodies were unearthed during excavations for a trolley line at the site of the old graveyard, including that of a man named Dave Mullen, who was “shot and killed in a row with some soldiers from old Fort Lincoln,” according to the newspaper.

In 1959, a shallow grave was discovered at the southwest section of the plot, where a new governor’s house was to be constructed. Two workers using a “power shovel” found the bones, the newspaper reported that year.

That same year, workers using a dirt loader found an “ancient pine box” holding the remains of a man who was believed to have died at 45. In total, at least five bodies were found that summer.

Archaeologists are now reviewing and cataloging the remains that were found in May. They expect to be done early in 2027.

A funeral home has been contracted to help with the reburials, and a nonprofit group was called to the site when the remains were found.

“We had a word of prayer over that site for the deceased,” Greg Carr, a chaplain with Crisis Care Chaplaincy, said in an interview this week.

He said the reburials will take place in the spring.

“We’ll handle the spiritual aspect of the events,” Mr. Carr said. “There’s no way to know who these people are or what their religious backgrounds were, if they even had one in the 1800s in North Dakota.”

Jennifer Sinco Kelleher contributed reporting.

item.title: A Vague, Redacted Execution Protocol in Tennessee Draws Scrutiny
item.description:
Last year, Tennessee’s lethal injection execution protocol underwent a striking transformation.

The manual laying out the procedure was slashed in half, stripped down from 104 pages in a previous version to 44 pages. Details about certain staff and the single drug now at the heart of the protocol were shrouded in secrecy.

And some directions were made vague or vanished altogether, including the requirement that execution teams practice inserting an IV line.

Tennessee has botched two of its three executions this year, mostly recently in the case of Christa Pike last month. Her case in particular has prompted a wave of questions about why the state has struggled to carry out death sentences, while some other states, such as Texas, have not.

The stark differences between the protocol put in place last year and the one before it, which was last updated in 2018, have emerged as a focus of scrutiny in Tennessee.

The granular, grim elements of an execution, especially by lethal injection, have taken on greater interest and importance in the aftermath of Ms. Pike’s botched execution, as more Americans wrestle with the morality and ethics of capital punishment.

Even as polls have shown a decline in support for the death penalty, some leaders continue to champion capital punishment. The Pentagon announced this week that the Army officer convicted in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting would be carried out in public and broadcast via a livestream.

Republicans in Tennessee, where they hold a supermajority, say they remain committed to carrying out death sentences. But they have said they will examine how capital punishment is carried out and will consider changing the lethal injection protocol or switching to a different execution method.

The Tennessee Department of Correction said it had followed every step of the protocol in Ms. Pike’s execution attempt, which has “consistently been effective.”

Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican who is in the final months of his second and last term in office, has paused all executions and ordered an investigation into Ms. Pike’s botched execution. U.S. Senator Marsha Blackburn, also a Republican and the front-runner to replace Mr. Lee, has called for the state to switch to the electric chair.

Cameron Sexton, the speaker of the Tennessee House, said that Ms Pike should still face execution and that the state intends to find a way to carry on with capital punishment. “We’ll look at different methods and alternatives, and then we’ll look at how to speed up the process,” Mr. Sexton said in an interview.

Ms. Pike, 50, was convicted in 1996 of the torture and murder of a classmate.

The Department of Correction declined to answer questions about the current protocol or its changes, citing pending litigation. During earlier lawsuits brought by other death row inmates, the agency cited attorney-client privilege and a protective order in refusing to allow staff members answer a number of questions, including about the development of the protocol, the qualifications of the execution staff and details about the drugs used.

After the botched Pike execution on Sept. 30, the agency’s commissioner, Frank Strada, who had led the development of the new lethal injection protocol, said he would step down later this month.

Ms. Pike’s lawyers had warned about possible issues with the execution protocol, especially given her small veins and underlying medical conditions. She survived two doses of the drug, pentobarbital, and remains hospitalized. Her lawyers on Thursday said she was able to walk with some assistance, but continues to struggle with concentration and memory.

Like in other states, Tennessee law prohibits the public identification of workers who carry out executions or any company that assists in procuring or preparing drugs for lethal injection. There are strict limits on who can witness an execution; cellphones and outside photos are prohibited; and only lawyers for the death row inmate can witness the insertion of IV lines.

“The idea is to keep it from being sensationalized,” said David Raybin, a Nashville lawyer who helped write Tennessee’s death penalty statute. But in switching to lethal injection, he added, “we’ve involved more people. We’ve made it more complex.”

Yet key details of the process appear masked in the current Tennessee protocol, compared with the previous one and with those of some other states that use lethal injection. In Tennessee’s previous protocol, from 2018, only five pages appeared to have been removed, mainly related to security details of the prison where executions are held. But in the current protocol, the state appears to have withheld details of staff roles and duties.

“It’s why we can say that secrecy is a big part of all botched executions,” said Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. “When we don’t understand what’s happening, there’s not the opportunity to ask the hard questions that get good answers.”

In 2022, Mr. Lee instituted a moratorium on executions, and there was an independent review of the Tennessee process. During a deposition last year, Mr. Strada said he estimated he had read the report two or three times.

Some recommendations — including providing a copy of the protocol to the chemical provider — were followed, he said. Some were not. He said he did not enlist an outside consultant with a pharmaceutical background to offer guidance over the lethal injection process, as the report had recommended.

“It was only a recommendation,” Mr. Strada said when asked at the time, according to excerpts from the deposition reviewed by The New York Times. “It wasn’t a requirement.”

Directly asked if there was any unwritten guidance, Mr. Strada said everything was contained within the protocol.

The Texas protocol, which also uses pentobarbital, requires that all members of the drug team have at least one year of professional experience and a new team member must be supervised through two executions.

In Florida, which carried out 40 percent of all executions in the United States in 2025, the protocol specifies the kinds of certification each team member involved with the lethal injection process should have. It also directs the team to prepare for contingencies, including issues finding a vein and what to do if the prisoner is not unconscious after the first drug is administered.

Tennessee’s protocol does not publicly list contingencies. It says execution staff members should be “currently certified, licensed and/or qualified within the United States to place IV lines,” but does not offer specifics.

There is also an absence of public details in Tennessee’s protocol about how to handle complications in the execution chamber. In Idaho, for example, where execution by either lethal injection or a firing squad is allowed, there is a requirement for outside medical services to be on site and provide any necessary aid, “including resuscitation efforts for the condemned person as needed.”

On Sept. 30, the night Ms. Pike was set to be executed, emergency medical services were called to the Nashville prison at 8:50 p.m., according to a Nashville Fire Department report, and the first unit arrived at 9:15 p.m. It was not clear if Ms. Pike, who could be heard breathing, received care before that arrival.

Jesus Jiménez contributed reporting.

item.title: Fact-Checking Senate Ads in Iowa, New Hampshire and North Carolina
item.description:
With less than a month to go until the November midterms, both parties have blanketed the airwaves with campaign ads in battleground states as they seek control over Congress.

In Iowa, New Hampshire and North Carolina — three of the most competitive Senate races in the country — candidates and groups supporting them have all spent millions on ads faulting their opposition with failing to curb the cost of living, a top issue for voters, among other attacks.

Here’s a fact check of some of those claims.

What Was Said

“Here are the facts. It’s Ashley Hinson who’s missed nearly 200 votes in Congress. Votes to crack down on child pornography, reduce crime and lower health care costs.”— Senate Majority PAC, a top Democratic super PAC, in an ad that began airing in September

This is misleading. Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican Senate candidate in Iowa, and various groups supporting her candidacy have spent millions of dollars on ads attacking Josh Turek, a state representative and the Democratic nominee, for missing 58 percent of votes in the Iowa legislature this year (the claim is accurate).

In response, Mr. Turek and groups that support him have retorted that Ms. Hinson, too, has a record of absenteeism in the House — including missing votes to lower health care costs — by making an apples-to-oranges comparison.

The Senate Majority PAC cited Ms. Hinson missing 33 roll-call votes — or recorded votes on the House floor — as well as 163 votes in various committees she sits on since January 2021, when she first entered office.

But typically, a missed vote refers to a roll-call vote on the House floor, and Ms. Hinson actually has a better attendance record than most members of Congress. According to GovTrack, a nonprofit website that tracks congressional activities, Ms. Hinson has missed 33 of 2,915 roll-call votes from January 2021 to September 2026. That’s about 1.1 percent, less than the median of 2.1 percent among current members in the House. This year, she has missed five out of 314 votes, about 1.6 percent.

“A missed vote is a missed vote, and Ashley Hinson missed nearly 200 of them during her time in Congress,” Lauren French, a spokeswoman for the Democratic group, said in a statement.

The tally in the ad included missed committee votes. Ms. Hinson missed a roll-call vote in the House Appropriations Committee on a specific proposal to increase funding for community-based violence prevention programs (the motion failed 28 to 34).

Senate Majority PAC said Ms. Hinson missed a voice vote on an amendment to increase funding for programs that combat the exploitation of children and another voice vote on extending medical education programs in rural areas. But it is not clear whether Ms. Hinson was present for those particular votes as, by definition, voice votes do not take attendance. Both amendments passed without any opposition.

Billy Fuerst, a spokesman for the Hinson campaign, argued that by the ad’s logic, there is no record of any member of Congress supporting those amendments since names and position were not logged. Morevoer, he said, Ms. Hinson voted to advance the funding bills that included the two provisions to the full House.

What Was Said

“Pappas voted to line the pockets of health insurers with billions of tax dollars. Pappas even voted against vital funding for rural and vulnerable hospitals. Bigger profits for big insurance, higher costs for you.”— No Going Back PAC, a Republican super PAC, in an ad that began airing in September

This is misleading. This ad attacking Representative Chris Pappas, the Democratic nominee for Senate in New Hampshire, describes his opposition to the Republicans’ signature tax cut and domestic spending package as a vote against funding for rural hospitals.

That characterization omits the bulk of what the legislation actually does (extend tax cuts and cut social safety net programs). And it ignores that a provision creating a fund for rural hospitals was largely included to address deep funding cuts to Medicaid that threatened rural hospitals.

The domestic spending legislation created a $50 billion fund for rural hospitals but also cut Medicaid spending in rural areas by $137 billion over a decade, according to an analysis by KFF, a health policy nonprofit. So while Mr. Pappas technically voted against the $50 billion fund, he also voted against the $137 billion cut to rural Medicaid spending.

The ad also cites Mr. Pappas’s support for legislation to extend extra subsidies for Obamacare as votes to “line the pockets of health insurers,” echoing a longstanding criticism.

Extra subsidies created in 2021 during the pandemic made health insurance less expensive for most people enrolled in plans under the Affordable Care Act, known as Obamacare. But despite Democratic efforts to extend them and Mr. Pappas’s support, those subsidies expired this year. As a result, millions of Americans have dropped Obamacare coverage, and premiums have increased for many more. Conservative critics have argued that the extra subsidies enriched insurers, even as premiums continued to increase.

The ad was funded by No Going Back PAC, a new super PAC with ties to MAGA Inc., President Trump’s main super PAC. The group said Mr. Pappas “should be ashamed” of his vote.

What Was Said

“I’m going to show you something. No A.I., no special effects, just Michael Whatley in his own words: ‘Grocery prices are down, gasoline prices are down, housing prices are down, inflation is down.’ Unbelievable. And so is this: ‘There is no inflation.’”— Former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic nominee for Senate in North Carolina, in an ad that began airing in September

This needs context. It’s true that the ad features remarks made by Michael Whatley, the Republican candidate, without special effects or enhancements by artificial intelligence. But the ad omits that those remarks occurred more than a year earlier, in an interview in July 2025, when overall prices were increasing at a slower pace and gas prices were stable.

At the time Mr. Whatley made those remarks, mortgage rates had dipped slightly and Mr. Trump’s war in Iran, and its accompanying surge in gas prices, was still months away. The New York Times had reported that inflation had accelerated, but remained relatively calm in the early months of the second Trump administration. Economists, though, were warning that the impact of Mr. Trump’s tariff policies would soon manifest in the form of higher prices.

The average price for gas in the country was $3.13 a gallon, not too different from the $3.10 a gallon at the end of January 2025, when Mr. Trump began his second term. Average 30-year mortgage rates had fallen to about 6.7 percent in July 2025 from about 7 percent that January.

“Prices were down considerably in 2025 from the record-setting inflation caused by Joe Biden’s reckless spending policies endorsed by Roy Cooper,” DJ Griffin, a spokesman for the Whatley campaign, said in a statement.

Still, Mr. Whatley was wrong that grocery prices, housing and inflation were “down” in the summer of 2025. The Consumer Price Index had risen by 2.7 percent in June 2025 from a year earlier, housing by 4 percent and food-at-home by 2.4 percent. Median home prices in June had also risen, albeit modestly, by 1.8 percent year-over-year, according to the National Association of Realtors.

In comparison, the C.P.I. increased by 3.4 percent this August, the latest available data, food-at-home by 2.2 percent and housing by 3.1 percent. In the first week of October, gas prices averaged $4.35, and mortgage rates were higher than when Mr. Trump took office.

The Cooper campaign said Mr. Whatley has for months engaged in a pattern of downplaying and making false statements about inflation, for example, saying in January that “there is no inflation” and in September that “we are not getting gouged” on gas prices.

item.title: Economic Pain and an Unpopular Trump Put G.O.P. on its Heels With Three Weeks to Go
item.description:
Three weeks from Election Day, deep frustration over an economy that feels unworkable for Americans at most every level, from farmers to truckers to consumers, has expanded the map of competitive electoral contests into areas that seemed safely Republican just a couple of months ago.

Sustained high prices are putting at risk some of the constituencies, states and congressional districts that President Trump and Republicans won decisively in 2024. The widespread discontent has prompted candidates, parties and major G.O.P. fund-raising groups to shift their messages and ad spending in crucial races to try to move voters in the final days of the midterm campaign.

With control of the House, Senate and the vast majority of the country’s governor’s offices and legislatures at stake, Republicans are examining their own deteriorating internal polling, along with their experiences with voters, and say they are reassessing their odds and triaging the map.

On Friday, for example, the leading Senate Republican super PAC began to plunge another $30 million into advertising in Texas to try to save the state’s Senate seat for Ken Paxton, the Republican attorney general.

Several races that are likely to determine the overall outcome on Election Day — the Maine and Michigan Senate elections, for example — remain tight. Control of the chamber could easily boil down to one or two of these razor-thin contests.

Still, Republican baggage is piling up, regionally and nationally. Mr. Trump is facing backlash to mass deportations in South Texas and South Florida. His party is bracing for anger at expanding data centers in states including Ohio and Michigan. In big farming states, record diesel prices have arrived just in time for harvest season. In colder northern states, spiking heating oil costs loom for families.

“When you’ve got a sitting president whose job approval rating is in the high 30s,” said Colin Reed, a veteran Republican strategist, “it makes it really difficult for any Republican candidate to compete and win.”

The White House is racing for stopgap solutions. Mr. Trump announced $90 payouts for millions of seniors on Medicare, and on Friday began sending $500 rebate checks he had promised for some Affordable Care Act customers. He has also promised a $5,000 check for every adult U.S. citizen if his party retains control of Congress. This week, in Nebraska — a typically solidly Republican state — Mr. Trump announced an executive order to loosen restrictions on the use of tax-free diesel on the roads.

On Friday, Mr. Trump said he would allow Russian diesel imports after years of sanctions, in an attempt to lower prices.

Mr. Trump’s unpopularity over his handling of the economy — one of his biggest strengths when he ran two years ago — is driving Republican troubles in a nationalized political environment.

The party still holds structural advantages over Democrats, including a Senate map with more contests in states that Mr. Trump won in 2024; redrawn congressional maps that made more seats favorable to the G.O.P.; and a wide financial lead, bolstered in part by Mr. Trump’s own powerful super PAC, MAGA Inc. In past elections, particularly when Mr. Trump has been on the ballot, some polls have underestimated his popularity.

Those advantages have provided little comfort to Republicans who see their candidates faltering in increasingly red corners of the nation.

The leading House Republican super PAC, the Congressional Leadership Fund, all but ceded the first Republican-held seat of the election this week, moving money out of a district in Nebraska where Representative Don Bacon is retiring. Mr. Bacon occupies the most Democratic-leaning seat of any Republican in the House.

In an interview, Mr. Bacon said he had urged party officials not to abandon the seat just yet.

“I wish they could have shown a little more patience,” he said. “The No. 1 issue is the president is not popular in the district.”

Republicans also recently pulled money from the Senate race in North Carolina, where Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican, is retiring. They redirected cash to Kansas and South Carolina, which remain a stretch for Democrats but would have seemed out of reach earlier this year. The top super PAC backing Senate Democrats, Senate Majority PAC, is reserving $5 million in ad time in Kansas.

“There are states right now in play that I would not have imagined being in play,” former President Barack Obama said at a fund-raiser for Democratic Senate nominees in Virginia on Wednesday, rattling off states such as Texas, Kansas and Nebraska.

“We could end up losing all of them by two points,” he added, according to excerpts released by his office, warning against Democratic complacency. “But we have a chance.”

Republicans, privately and publicly, are concerned about an enthusiasm gap. Culture war issues, such as transgender athletes’ rights, are still in heavy rotation in Republican ads. But polls show voters are focused squarely on their deep unhappiness with the direction of an economy that Mr. Trump had promised to fix.

“Angry people vote and satisfied people don’t,” Mike Johnson, the Republican House speaker, warned a crowd at a diner this week in Nazareth, Pa. He said Republicans had successfully closed the border from unauthorized immigrants, but the achievement had pushed the issue out of mind.

Mr. Johnson, typically an optimist, later in the week mused to Fox News aloud about what he might do if his party were to lose the majority this fall. “If God moves on our hearts and says we should, you know, go back to my hometown of Shreveport and start a lawn business, I’ll do that with equal fervor,” he said.

Mr. Trump has traveled in red states, including three times to Texas over the past month, with another visit by Vice President JD Vance planned for next week. They hope to get Trump supporters who typically vote only in presidential elections to also vote in the midterms. The president has repeatedly urged them to act as though his name were on the ballot.

The challenge with that plan, said Paul Shumaker, a Republican strategist in North Carolina, is that many of those voters vote on the economy.

“The lower-income, blue-collar voters that Donald Trump brought to his winning coalition for Republicans is the demographic group of voters who are being impacted most by the higher energy costs,” Mr. Shumaker said.

Recent New York Times/Siena University polls of red states show Democrats also doing well with younger voters, older voters, independent voters and Latino voters who backed Mr. Trump in 2024.

Still, Republicans could flip the Kansas governorship, which Democrats have held for eight years. And Democrats face unexpectedly competitive statewide races in Minnesota, which has not elected a Republican in a statewide election since 2006, when Gov. Tim Pawlenty won re-election.

Mr. Pawlenty said the state has offset some of the tough national political environment for Republicans in part because voters there blame a spate of fraud scandals on Democrats.

“Democrats are trying to make the election a referendum on President Trump while the Republicans are trying to make it a referendum on fraud,” Mr. Pawlenty said in an email.

Democrats in states like North Carolina vividly remember past elections where they expected to win or win comfortably only to lose or win by razor-thin margins. Republicans remember them, too. Austin Barbour, a Republican strategist based in Mississippi, invoked a quote made famous by his uncle, Haley Barbour, a former Republican National Committee chairman, to describe the political climate: “It’s never as bad as it seems or as good as it seems.”

The younger Mr. Barbour said he believed Republicans would ultimately prevail in states that are historically Republican, in part because of “the level of far-left candidates that the Democrats are nominating.”

But cries about looming socialism are proving a tough sell when voters are unhappy now.

Sarah Trone Garriott, a Democratic state senator and Lutheran minister who is trying to flip an Iowa congressional seat, said a farmer told her it would cost $16,000 more this year to harvest his crop because of higher diesel costs. That was after dealing with tariffs in the farm market and higher costs for fertilizer, which made spring planting more expensive.

“I was at the Labor Day parade, and I had a union member say to me, ‘My parents told me if you vote for Republicans, your life will get better,’” she recounted. “And he said, ‘It isn’t getting better: We’ve got dirty water; we’ve got cancer; we’ve got higher costs. I’m voting all Democrat this year.’”

On Friday, the Cook Political Report moved Mr. Nunn’s seat to “lean Democratic.”

Ms. Trone Garriott said the evidence that Iowa Democrats are doing well is not merely anecdotal: Representative Zach Nunn, the two-term Republican she is trying to unseat, voted in Congress last month to end the Iran war or seek congressional authorization to continue it — after having campaigned with Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, just a month earlier.

Jim Runestad, a state senator and the chairman of the Michigan Republican Party, said it was smart for former Representative Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee, and other Republican candidates to distance themselves from the president. Mr. Rogers has supported a one-year moratorium on data center developments in Michigan and called for an end to the Iran war and to what he has called the “tariff war.”

“You shouldn’t walk in lock step,” Mr. Runestad said. “In an off-year election when the president of your party is in office,” he added, “there is always a headwind.”

The next three weeks will determine whether seeking that distance this late in the campaign season will be enough.

State Representative Carrie Rheingans, a progressive Michigan Democrat, has been campaigning across the state for Democrats including Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the party’s Senate nominee. In past election years, she said, Trump voters “wanted somebody to come in and make things different because it wasn’t working.” Now, they have been let down again, she said.

That dejection created an opening for the left. “The voters are just tired of big corporations,” she said. “They’re either price-gouging us, or they’re monopolies.”

Vince Bjorling, a retired doctor from Scottsbluff, Neb., said he planned to vote for the Democratic nominee for governor and independent candidates for House and Senate.

Mr. Bjorling, a former Republican who said he left the party early in the Trump era, said he had volunteered for a independent House campaign and had encountered “a lot of people out there who are very, very angry with the policies that the president has put forward, and also our representatives basically falling in line.”

“The tariffs were a big problem, because that created affordability problems,” he said. “The war in Iran was miscalculated and misguided, and now has led to even more affordability issues.”

Republicans “can’t run on the issues,” he said, “and they can’t run on their record.”

Mitch Smith contributed reporting.

item.title: Executions Are Again on the Minds of a Divided Public
item.description:
Within the span of eight days, the country has learned of a failed execution and a successful execution, and has been promised a livestreamed execution by military firing squad before year’s end.

The most severe form of criminal punishment — there are roughly 2,000 people on death row nationwide — execution has taken center stage in a nation already split politically and culturally, amplifying divisions just weeks before a pivotal midterm election.

Death penalty opponents have seized upon the blundered attempt to kill Christa Pike in Tennessee last week to push for an end to the death penalty. Conversely, the nation’s top military official said on Thursday that the United States would carry out the government’s first public execution since 1936.

The announcement from the Pentagon chief, Pete Hegseth, and its timing, exemplify the salient place that the death penalty has taken in the nation’s polarized political landscape in President Trump’s second term.

On the day Mr. Trump returned to office, he urged prosecutors across the country to pursue and carry out capital punishment. In 2025, states executed more people than they had since 2009, largely driven by a sharp jump in Florida under Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican.

The failed execution of Ms. Pike — who survived two doses of pentobarbital that may have been injected improperly — has galvanized death penalty opponents, who have denounced what they see as a grisly example of capital punishment’s faults.

And the two events together have brought the issue of the death penalty — something that has for decades taken place in hidden rooms inside mostly rural prisons — back into the forefront of Americans’ minds.

“What we’re seeing is the brutality of the institution of the death penalty coming back into public focus,” said Mark Osler, a law professor at the University of St. Thomas in Minneapolis who has studied the death penalty. “Tennessee didn’t intend to do that; the federal government does.”

“Given that there has been a rise in executions,” he added, “it’s a good time to have that debate.”

Nearly 1,700 people have been executed in the past 50 years, including Jamaal Howard, 46, who was put to death on Wednesday in Texas, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, with a peak of 98 killed in 1999. Mr. Howard had been convicted of murdering Vickie Swartout, 42, during a 2000 robbery. Tennessee had sought to execute Ms. Pike for her 1995 killing of her classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.

While 27 states retain the death penalty, fewer than half of those have carried out an execution in the past five years. Virginia abolished the penalty in 2021, and Ohio’s Republican governor, Mike DeWine, said in June that he wanted his state to do so as well.

In modern times, lethal injection has been used far more than any other method, though states have turned to alternative methods — both new and old — in recent years. Several have authorized the firing squad, and two, Alabama and Louisiana, have used the novel method of asphyxiation via nitrogen.

Public opinion polls have shown support for the death penalty steadily declining in recent decades, though a majority of Americans still support it. One poll from this past summer found that two-thirds were in favor.

Still, the specter of livestreaming the execution of Nidal Hasan, a former Army major who was convicted of murdering 13 people — mostly soldiers — and wounding dozens more at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009, has upset many who might otherwise support his killing.

“Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting,” Senator Thom Tillis, Republican of North Carolina, wrote on social media. “Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.”

Mr. Hasan, now 56, was motivated by his radical views of Islam to carry out the killings in retaliation for America’s wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. He was wounded by responding police officers and is now paralyzed from the waist down, raising the possibility that he could be transported in a wheelchair to his execution, which is scheduled for Dec. 3. Mr. Hegseth said Mr. Hasan would be killed at Fort Hood around the same time of day — early afternoon — that he committed the crimes.

The reactions to the announcement fell largely along ideological lines — Republicans are much more likely to support capital punishment — but were far from uniform, underscoring the complexity of the issue.

Some Roman Catholic leaders condemned the execution plans. The Catholic Church has long opposed the death penalty as part of its theological commitment to humans across their life spans, though recently U.S. bishops have prioritized ending abortion and defending immigrants.

Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, the president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, called the planned livestream “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death” and warned it would harm the country.

“The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people,” he said.

Vice President JD Vance, an atheist turned Catholic, said on Friday that he would not watch the execution if it was livestreamed and also cast doubt on that idea, saying, “I don’t know if that’s actually going to happen.”

But in a sign of the continued sharp divide that the Trump movement has carved in American Christianity, an energetic cohort of right-wing Christians defended the livestream on biblical grounds.

Josh Howerton, the pastor of Lakepointe Church, an evangelical congregation with locations in and around Dallas, argued on social media that executions in the Bible were carried out publicly as deterrents.

“I do not think you can say it’s unbiblical or automatically wrong,” he said of public executions, noting passages that described public stonings.

The prospect of a public execution was raised prominently around the turn of the century, when some proposed televising the killing of Timothy McVeigh.

Mr. McVeigh, convicted of carrying out the Oklahoma City bombing in 1995 that killed 168 people, himself had urged as much in a letter to The Oklahoman newspaper in which he argued for “equal access” to his execution: “A reasonable solution seems obvious: hold a true ‘public’ execution — allow a public broadcast.”

In the end, he was executed by lethal injection at an Indiana prison in 2001, with a couple of dozen people watching his death in person and about 232 more — including survivors and their relatives — viewing on closed-circuit television from Oklahoma City.

Notably, Mr. Hasan has said he wants to be killed for his crimes, saying he sees an opportunity for martyrdom, though he does not appear to expect the firing squad or a public death.

“I’m paraplegic and could be in jail for the rest of my life,” he told a military panel in 2010. “However, if I died by lethal injection I would still be a martyr.”

Emily Cochrane contributed reporting from Nashville, and Elizabeth Dias from Washington.
